title: No requests today
hook: on Shabbat the weekday requests are replaced by one blessing of the day's holiness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 92, the Sabbath song that never says Sabbath. Your line was good to give thanks. Who did you thank for something steady? Today, what Shabbat takes out of the prayer book. Day six hundred seventeen.

Think about what you ask for in a normal week. Help me understand this. Forgive me for that. Heal my friend. Help with money. Fix this mess. Most of us run on requests. The weekday Amidah is the same. We walked through it earlier this year: a prayer of nineteen blessings, and the long middle is one request after another. Wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good year's harvest, justice, peace. Then Friday night comes, you open the prayer book to the same place, and the middle is gone.
screen: `WE RUN ON REQUESTS.` → `NINETEEN BLESSINGS ON A WEEKDAY.` → `ON SHABBAT, THE MIDDLE IS GONE.`

segments.voice: On Shabbat, the Amidah keeps its first three blessings, the praise, and its last three, the thanks and the peace. But the thirteen requests in the middle are taken out. In their place goes a single blessing called kedushat hayom, the holiness of the day. So the Sabbath Amidah has seven blessings instead of nineteen. Why remove the requests? The rabbis give a few reasons. One is that asking for your needs means thinking about everything that's wrong: illness, debt, the harvest. And on Shabbat, they said, you shouldn't be weighed down by that. The day isn't for fixing your life. It's for living it as if it were already enough. There's a striking line in the Talmud about visiting the sick on Shabbat. You don't pray at length for their recovery. Instead, one teacher said, you tell them: it's Shabbat, we don't cry out; healing will come soon. The day itself is the comfort. That doesn't mean people stop caring on Shabbat, or stop hoping. Hearts still carry their worries in. The rabbis noticed that too, and some of their sources struggle with how much request is allowed. But the shape of the prayer makes a point. Six days a week you're a person with needs. One day a week, the prayer treats you as a person who has what they need. You come before God not to ask, but just to be there. The middle blessing is the day itself.
screen: `NINETEEN BECOMES SEVEN.` · `ONE BLESSING: THE DAY'S HOLINESS.` · `NOT WEIGHED DOWN BY NEEDS.` · `HEALING WILL COME SOON.` · then, large: `NO REQUESTS TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go an hour without asking for anything. Start now, with the sit. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, don't ask for a single thing, not from God, not from yourself. No fix, no plan, no wish. When a request comes up, and it will, notice it, set it down beside you, and come back to the breath. Just be in what is. Then try to carry that for the next hour. The bell holds the time.
No requests today. On Shabbat the thirteen weekday requests give way to one blessing of the day's holiness.
Your line: no requests today. For one hour today, ask for nothing, and notice how often you want to. Day six hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: The Shabbat Amidah has seven blessings: the first three and last three of the weekday Amidah, with the thirteen petitions replaced by one central blessing for the holiness of the day, worded differently at each Shabbat service.
